title: A runoff multiplier fitted in 1997-2009 reduced 2010-2021 annual prediction error by 39% at 156 south-east Australian catchments
abstract: We tested whether a proportional runoff reduction gives a useful description of the persistent south-east Australian runoff deficit. We used annual CAMELS-AUS v2.03 data and fitted each catchment's relation to current and prior rain on 1951-1996. A shared runoff multiplier fitted only on 1997-2009 was 0.722. Applied unchanged to 2010-2021 at 156 catchments, it reduced mean squared error by 39.4% against the unchanged relation (conditional three-year block interval 30.3-45.3%). A fixed runoff offset gave a 20.7% reduction. An offset plus multiplier and an extra rain term gave no clear further error reduction. The multiplier gain held with SILO rain, a quadratic baseline and rain-range screening, but its advantage over an offset was uncertain in two checks. Within-era tests also favored scaling after 1997. We prove that proportional runoff loss lowers the absolute rain slope while leaving fractional rain elasticity unchanged. Thus slope loss alone cannot identify a new response shape. The regional affine intercept was positive in spatial resamples, so exact proportional scaling is not established. Annual models, inherited catchment selection, short test records, fixed-baseline uncertainty and the retrospective transfer-test choice limit inference. This is conditional runoff prediction with observed rain, not an operational forecast or a causal explanation.

display.caption: Corrections fitted in 1997-2009 predict 2010-2021 runoff with observed rain. All configurations use 156 shared catchments. Lower error is better.
